A brand new agency isn’t necessarily bad… but the risk profile is very different.

2️⃣ Where are they in product-market fit?
Are they testing?
Selling?
Or already stable?
Each stage requires a different type of operator.

Are people staying?
Or is LinkedIn showing a revolving door?

4️⃣ Do they have a clear salary structure and budget?
If compensation feels improvised… the business probably is too.

The funny thing is:
Most of this information can be stalked online in 5 minutes.
But I strongly encourage candidates to ask these questions directly.

Not like an FBI interrogation.
Just genuine curiosity.
You’re not trying to catch them out.
You’re trying to understand the stage, the potential, and the reality.

Because the wrong GTM role doesn’t just waste your time.
It can damage your momentum.

I'm becoming increasingly convinced companies are picking job titles out of a hat.

Years ago, one of the selling points of a recruiter was access.

We had access to talent databases you didn't.

Today?

We have the opposite problem.

There are almost TOO many people we could potentially reach.

And as AI changes roles, I'm seeing companies layer more and more responsibilities into one position.

Then we try to represent all of those responsibilities in the title.

So we end up with:
• GTM
• Revenue
• Operations
• Systems
• AI
• Automation
• Engineering

Throw 4 in a blender.
Voilà. Oui Oui. New job title.

Except now you've created a role nobody searches for.

Candidates don't recognise themselves in it.

Recruiters don't know what comparable profiles look like.

Hiring managers start looking for a combination of skills that may barely exist in the market.

And suddenly we're hunting a unicorn based on a job title we invented 3 weeks ago.

This is becoming a real challenge across:
• GTM Engineering
• RevOps
• Sales Ops
• Revenue Systems
• Sales Enablement
• Growth

My biggest recommendation to companies hiring in these functions right now:
Keep the title simple.

Put the complexity in the job description, not the job title.

Before you start searching, get painfully clear on:
• What this person owns
• What they need to build
• What problems they're solving
• What skills are genuinely essential
• What outcomes you expect from them

Because in an emerging function, you don't have decades of precedent to fall back on.

Definition before title.

Otherwise your next GTM hire might genuinely require a job reveal 🎈

This is a conversation I have weekly, if not daily, with clients and candidates.

Most BDMs were responsible for building their own pipeline.

More BDMs had SDRs supporting them with pipeline generation.

Did the SDR suddenly appear out of nowhere?
Not really.

The responsibilities got split across more specialised roles.

A lot of the work already existed across:
• RevOps
• Sales Ops
• Outbound
• Growth
• Marketing Ops
• CRM Architecture
• Revenue Systems
• Automation

The market just started grouping some of those responsibilities under a shiny new title:
GTM Engineer.

So you don't necessarily need to "become a GTM Engineer" if you've spent years building revenue systems in RevOps, Sales Ops, Outbound or CRM Architecture.

You may have already been doing GTM Engineering.

Now before someone comes for me with:
"BUT IT IS DIFFERENT."

Yes, individual roles are different.

That's exactly the point.

What's different is the job description.

One GTM Engineer might own outbound infrastructure.

Another might build AI agents.

Another might basically be a Revenue Systems Engineer.

Another might sit closer to Growth.

Realistically, the job title tells me very little.

The job description tells me everything.

Stop obsessing over whether your previous title says "GTM Engineer."

Look at the problems you've solved.

That's where the real match is.

The quickest way to increase your GTM Engineer salary might be the thing that eventually kills your career progression.

6 months. New job. 20% raise. Repeat. Until the market stops rewarding you.

One way you might be shooting your GTM Engineer career in the foot:

Jumping too quickly from role to role.

Right now, GTM Engineering is HOT.

Salaries are high.

Demand is high.

Companies are fighting over experienced talent.

So naturally…

6 months in one role.

Another company offers more money.

Jump.

8 months later, better title.

Jump again.

For a while?

It works.

Until the market cools down.

And suddenly, companies have more choice and your CV shows:

6 months.

8 months.

4 months.

10 months.

Now you’re plateauing.

And GTM Engineering particularly needs tenure.

You can’t build a great system in 3 months.

You need time to see:

• Did Sales actually adopt it?
• Did it generate revenue?
• What broke when you scaled it?
• What did you change after V1 failed?
• Did it still work 12 months later?
• Could you adapt it when the GTM strategy changed?

Building teaches you technical skills.

Staying long enough to see what happens teaches you judgement.

And judgement is what companies pay senior GTM Engineers for.

Someone with +3 years inside one scaling SaaS company may have lived through:

$5M → $20M ARR.

50 → 200 employees.

One GTM motion → three.

One CRM architecture → “who the hell built this?” → rebuild.

They’ve seen consequences.

And consequences create judgement.

I’m not saying stay somewhere you’re miserable.

I’m saying don’t let a hot market convince you that every salary increase is career progression.

Because markets change.

And when reality hits, tenure might be the thing companies start paying a premium for.

I'm a recruiter. Why the hell am I learning MCP? 😂
Because I recruit GTM Engineers.
 
And I've realised something over the last 2 years:
I can't recruit people doing this work if I don't understand the work.
 
Not just the buzzwords.
 
Actually understand it.
 
So I'm constantly learning about:
 
• Outbound infrastructure
• Deliverability
• Enrichment
• APIs
• AI agents
• Automation
• RevOps strategy
• And now... MCP
 
Do I need to become better at building outbound systems than the GTM Engineers I recruit?
 
Absolutely not.
 
That would be concerning for everyone involved. 😂
 
But I need to understand:
 
• What good looks like
• What's actually difficult
• What's becoming commoditised
• What companies are trying to build
• What separates someone who knows the tools from someone who understands the system
 
Because otherwise, how am I supposed to interview them?
 
And this week I've been learning by actually building.
 
We've built this playbook with La Growth Machine and Firat Berber (thanks Brice Maurln and Mahé ABERLIN) around turning LinkedIn event attendees into qualified outbound opportunities.
 
And that's what I love about recruiting in this space.
 
My candidates are learning constantly.

My clients are learning constantly.
 
So I have to learn constantly too.
 
The minute I stop understanding how GTM is changing, I become another recruiter searching LinkedIn for "Clay" AND "Apollo" AND "Salesforce" and hoping for the best.
 
And nobody needs that. 😂

Back to MCP I go. 🫡

content:
Change your job title to GTM Engineer if...
...you're already doing the job.

I've noticed the same pattern over and over again this week.

Candidates from SaaS companies tell me:
"I'm struggling to find GTM Engineer opportunities."

Then I open their LinkedIn profile.

Their title says:
• Marketing Automation or vague mix of RevOps and Growth
• Automation Specialist

But after speaking to them...

They're clearly GTM Engineers.

Here's the problem.

Recruiters don't search by responsibilities.

They search by job title.

If I search for "GTM Engineer", and your profile doesn't contain those words...
You simply don't appear.

I know you exist because I'm the only one to niche into that industry/role but not other recruiters!

The irony?
You're probably spending your days teaching clients how to enrich data, improve targeting, and make themselves easier to find.

Meanwhile...

Your own LinkedIn profile isn't optimized.

Treat your profile like you would a prospect database.

Would you launch outbound against contacts with:
❌ the wrong job title
❌ outdated information
❌ missing keywords

Of course not.
So don't do it to yourself.

If you're already:
• building automations
• connecting APIs
• owning CRM architecture
• designing AI workflows
• supporting revenue through systems
• Managing outbound campaigns
...make sure your profile reflects it.

Because the best opportunity in the world can't find you if you're hiding behind yesterday's job title.

Your LinkedIn profile is just another database.

Optimize it like a GTM Engineer would.

What would you add?

Something genuinely shocks me when interviewing GTM Engineers:

How many are missing the basics of deliverability!

You can build an AI agent but you don't know why your emails are landing in spam?

We have a problem

I interview people who can

-> Build complex Clay tables.
-> Create AI agents.
-> Connect 17 tools together.
-> Talk about MCP.

Then I ask:

“Your reply rate suddenly drops to 0%. What do you do?”

And sometimes the answer is:

"The inboxes are burned. Replace them."

Your outbound is a system.
Your job isn't to guess what broke.
Your job is to diagnose it.

Before you burn time replacing mailboxes, isolate the variable.

Run a placement test using completely neutral, plain text with zero links or sales pitch.

If that neutral email lands in the primary inbox, your mailboxes aren't burned at all. Your campaign copy or links were the problem.

Strong GTM Engineers look for signals before tearing down infrastructure.

This is why my candidates run outbound mailboxes on Maildoso.

They manage around 30 of their dedicated mailboxes per clients across their campaigns.

They provide the BEST sending infrastructure with in-house IP rotation and self-healing mailboxes that rotate automatically, so deliverability stays over 95%.

When you know the infrastructure itself isn't the variable, you can move down the diagnostic chain with confidence:

Investigate the list.
The targeting.
The copy.
The offer.

AI can help you build faster.

It can also help you build the wrong thing faster 

GTM Engineers: replies suddenly drop to 0%. What's the FIRST thing you check?

They get hired because they understand how hiring actually works.

Every week, I interview founders, CROs and GTM leaders hiring for some of the fastest-growing SaaS companies.

I also speak to hundreds of GTM candidates.

Here's what I've learned.

Most people focus on getting an interview.

The best candidates focus on making the hiring manager's decision easier.

That means:
• Understanding what the company is actually trying to solve.
• Positioning your experience around those problems.
• Reaching out to the right people instead of relying on Easy Apply.
• Reading between the lines of a job description.

A job description is rarely just a list of responsibilities.

It's a roadmap of the company's biggest pain points.

That's exactly why I'm launching a weekly newsletter.

Every week, I'll break down one real GTM Engineering or Growth role from the market and cover:
